core: the working definition, attributed: a bond is a loan an investor makes to a borrower, usually a government or a company, in tradable form (Investor.gov working definition, echoed by OpenStax and CFI)
the three named parts: face value (par value), coupon (interest), and maturity date — each with one line and an original example
how bonds pay: regular interest (coupon) payments during the bond's life plus the principal back at maturity
bond prices and rates: prices move inversely with interest rates, stated simply (interest-rates is a sibling topic)
risk in bonds: default risk and interest-rate risk, each named with one line
bonds vs stocks: lending versus owning, stated simply (stocks is a sibling topic)
the honest framing: bonds are loans with a paper trail
supporting: bonds as tradable investments that can be bought and sold before maturity (marketable securities)
government versus corporate bonds: Treasury securities backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government; corporate bonds carry more default risk
bonds as fixed-income securities because their payments are set in advance
the indenture as the legal contract that names the bond's terms

claims.claim: A bond is a debt security: a loan an investor makes to a borrower, usually a government or a company, in a form that can be bought and sold. Investor.gov: when you buy a bond, you are lending to the issuer, which may be a government, municipality, or corporation; CFI: the issuer borrows capital from the bondholder; OpenStax: the bond purchaser is the lender and the issuer is the borrower.

Face value (par value) is the principal amount the issuer promises to repay at maturity; it is the amount the bond is worth at the end of its term. OpenStax: par value equals the principal the issuer will repay at the maturity date; CFI: principal (or face value) is the initial amount of money invested in the bond; Investor.gov: the issuer repays the principal, also known as face value or par value, when the bond matures.

The coupon is the regular interest payment on a bond, computed from the coupon rate applied to the face value. Coupon rates are always stated in annual terms (even when payments are semiannual or quarterly) and usually stay fixed for the bond's life. OpenStax example: a $1,000 bond at a 5% coupon rate pays $50 per year.
The maturity date is the expiration date of the bond: when the term ends, the issuer makes the final interest (coupon) payment and repays the principal, or face value.

A bondholder receives two kinds of cash flow: periodic coupon (interest) payments during the bond's life and repayment of the principal at maturity. OpenStax: the two sides of a bond investment are the payment of the par value at maturity and the periodic coupon payments, both contractually determined.

Bond prices and market interest rates move in opposite directions: when interest rates fall, bond prices rise, and when interest rates rise, bond prices fall. OpenStax: bond price and interest rate have an inverse relationship, with floating-rate bonds as an exception.

Bonds are tradable: they can be bought and sold before maturity. TreasuryDirect: 'marketable' means you can transfer the security to someone else and sell it before it matures. OpenStax: a bond is an investment that can be bought and sold.

Default risk is the risk that the borrower fails to pay the promised interest or principal. CFI: default is when an individual or entity cannot pay the pre-specified amount of interest or principal. U.S. Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, and OpenStax notes the likelihood of default on them is remote; corporate bonds carry more risk because a corporation cannot raise taxes to cover its debts.

Interest-rate risk is the risk that changes in market interest rates change a bond's price; it applies even to the most reliable borrowers because a fixed coupon becomes more or less attractive as rates move. Investor.gov names interest rate risk among the types of risk that affect investments.

Bonds versus stocks is lending versus owning: a bondholder is a lender with a promised schedule of payments, while a stockholder owns a piece of the company and shares in what remains after lenders are paid. Investor.gov: buying a bond means lending to the issuer; CFI: the issuer borrows capital from the bondholder.

Bonds are called fixed-income securities because they provide a set amount of cash inflow to their owners, with payments clearly stated in the bond agreement. OpenStax: because bonds provide a set amount of cash inflow to their owners, they are often called fixed-income securities.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame bonds differently: Investor.gov calls a bond a debt security 'similar to an IOU' with the buyer as lender; CFI emphasizes that the issuer borrows capital from the bondholder; OpenStax frames buying a bond as buying a future cash flow stream the issuer promises to make.
positions: Bond as IOU / loan from investor to borrower (Investor.gov)
Bond as borrowing by the issuer from the bondholder (CFI)
Bond as a promised future cash flow stream (OpenStax)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The framings are complementary views of the same instrument. The lesson uses Investor.gov's lending definition as the working definition (attributed) and folds in CFI's borrowing and OpenStax's cash-flow framings as supporting views.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How safe is U.S. government debt? CFI says the U.S. government's debt is 'considered risk-free,' while OpenStax says only that the likelihood of default is 'remote' and TreasuryDirect says securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government.
positions: Securities backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government (TreasuryDirect)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids claiming any bond is risk-free. It teaches that Treasury securities carry very low default risk because of government backing, while interest-rate risk applies to every bond.

sourceRecords.title: Bonds (Investor.gov Glossary)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Investor.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. securities regulator). The live glossary page returns HTTP 200 but renders its definition via JavaScript; the definition text was read from a Wayback Machine capture of the equivalent glossary entry (2018-09-17 snapshot, same text). Supports the working definition: a bond is a debt security similar to an IOU; borrowers issue bonds to raise money from investors willing to lend; buying a bond means lending to the issuer, which may be a government, municipality, or corporation; the issuer promises a specified rate of interest during the life of the bond and repayment of the principal (face value or par value) at maturity. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 10.1: Characteristics of Bonds
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; aiIngestionAllowed:false per subject source-map, so read via direct HTTP fetch on 2026-08-21 and restated in original prose). Supports: the bond purchaser as lender and issuer as borrower (Apple $1,000, 5%, 20-year example); par value as the principal repaid at maturity; coupon rate as the annual rate used to compute coupon payments ($1,000 x 5% = $50); coupon rates stated in annual terms and typically fixed for the bond's life; maturity date as the expiration when the final interest payment and principal are paid; the two sides of a bond investment (periodic coupons plus par value at maturity); the inverse relationship between bond prices and interest rates (rates fall, prices rise, and vice versa), with floating-rate notes as an exception; bonds as fixed-income securities that can be bought and sold; Treasury securities backed by the U.S. government with a remote likelihood of default; corporate bonds carrying more risk than government bonds because corporations cannot raise taxes. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About Treasury Marketable Securities
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of the Treasury, TreasuryDirect
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (official U.S. Treasury). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: all Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government; 'marketable' means the security can be transferred to someone else and sold before it matures; Treasury notes pay interest every six months; Treasury bills are short-term and sold at a discount from face value; Treasury bonds are long-term (historically 30-year, now also 20-year). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Bonds (Corporate Finance Institute)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: bonds as fixed-income securities issued by corporations and governments to raise capital; the issuer borrowing capital from the bondholder and making payments at a fixed or variable interest rate for a specified period; the indenture as the binding contract between issuer and bondholder; principal (face value) as the initial amount invested; maturity as the date the bond expires and principal must be paid; the coupon rate as the interest payments made to the bondholder; default as failing to pay the pre-specified interest or principal; U.S. government debt widely considered low-default because the government can raise taxes and print money; zero-coupon bonds as paying no coupons and issued at a discount. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
